comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

issues.descricao: Admin add_members pushes every username into group.users without skipping existing members, so adding someone already in the group hits the unique group_users index, returns a 500 and leaves earlier users partially added.
The public group members endpoint takes `limit` from params with no upper bound or positivity check, letting a visitor request huge pages or trigger a 500 with a negative limit.
Admin remove_member calls group.users.delete with a raw integer id, which raises RecordNotFound (404/500) when the user is not or no longer a member, e.g. on concurrent removal.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym is called before .uniq.compact, so a nil/blank default raises NoMethodError instead of being compacted away. WHY: During boot/DB outage default_locale is not guaranteed loaded (per PR description), so every fallback lookup and every request via ensure_loaded! crashes instead of falling back to :en. HOW: Compact/map safely, e.g. [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en].map{|l| l.try(:to_sym)}.compact.uniq.

WHAT: Raw request locale (user-controlled via User#effective_locale) is returned unsanitized in the fallback chain and interpolated into Regexp.new("\\.#{locale}\\.yml$") in load_locale. WHY: An attacker who sets locale to a regex metachar string (e.g. ".*") matches every file in I18n.load_path, forcing the server to load all locale files into memory on their request (resource exhaustion) and broadening the file-load surface. HOW: Normalize/allowlist the locale (to_sym + check against LocaleSiteSetting.supported_locales, fallback to :en) before returning it and before building the grep Regexp (use Regexp.escape).

WHAT: set_locale now synchronously loads up to 3 locale YAML files via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! on every request, and FallbackLocaleList#[] hits SiteSetting.default_locale on every fallback-miss lookup. WHY: First requests after boot/change block the request path on file I/O under LOAD_MUTEX, and every missing translation pays a SiteSetting lookup plus up to 3 backend lookups, amplifying hot-path cost. HOW: Memoize the resolved default locale per request/boot and keep per-request ensure_loaded! cheap (rely on @loaded_locales check), or preload fallbacks outside the request path.

SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym is evaluated before .compact, so if default_locale is nil the fallback lookup raises NoMethodError instead of falling back to [:en]. Compact first, then convert to symbols.

issues.descricao: Fallback locale catalogs are only loaded in the controller's set_locale filter, while translate loads just the current locale, so translations outside requests (jobs, mailers) cannot fall back to the site default or English.

comentarios.texto: Fallback catalogs are ensured loaded only in the controller filter, leaving non-controller translation paths without the catalogs required by the newly enabled fallback backend. Jobs::Base sets I18n.locale directly and PostAlerter uses I18n.with_locale, while the accelerator loads only the current locale and backend fallback lookups bypass that loader; missing keys therefore still produce missing translations or skip the configured site fallback until another request happens to load those catalogs. Ensure the full fallback chain is loaded at the translation boundary, rather than relying solely on the controller filter.

The new fallbacks contract requires the fallback locales (site default and :en, from FallbackLocaleList#[]) to be loaded before Backend::Simple#translate is asked for them — Backend::Simple only returns already-loaded translations. This PR added I18n.ensure_loaded!/I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! but wired it only into ApplicationController#set_locale, and the loader that actually gates every translation, I18n.translate (line 68), still loads only `config.locale`. As a result, any I18n.t performed outside the request cycle (console, background jobs, mailers) or before set_locale runs will not load the fallback locales and will silently return 'translation missing' instead of the fallback the new I18n.fallbacks advertises. Fix: have translate ensure the fallback chain is loaded (e.g. call I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! / load the fallback locales here), not rely on the controller hook.

translate loads only config.locale, but the new fallback chain (default_locale, :en) is loaded only by the controller's I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Outside controllers (jobs, mailers, rake), a key missing in the current locale falls back to a locale that is not loaded, so it returns 'translation missing', and the LRU cache then stores that result. Fix: in translate, call I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! (or load each locale in fallbacks[config.locale]) before the lookup.

issues.descricao: The translation cache key does not include the site or its default locale, but fallback results now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale, so multisite processes or a changed default locale serve stale fallback translations.

comentarios.texto: The new fallback order depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the accelerator's translation cache does not include that setting or the current site in its key. In a multisite process, two sites with the same user locale and different default locales reuse the first site's cached fallback translation; changing the default locale also leaves cached fallback results stale. Include the effective fallback chain or site/default-locale context in the translation cache key.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice does a separate CountDevices check then a separate INSERT with no lock/transaction. WHY: Two concurrent requests can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured device limit and breaking the enforcement invariant. HOW: Hold a lock/transaction across check-and-insert or enforce via DB constraint and map violation to ErrDeviceLimitReached.

WHAT: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever rowsAffected==0, which includes an existing device_id whose updated_at is older than 30 days (outside the BETWEEN window). WHY: A returning device after expiry can never re-register when the limit is hit, even though it is an update not a new device, and not-found is conflated with limit-reached.

WHAT: tagDeviceUI does localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice and never deletes on error, while TagDevice now propagates the error. WHY: After one ErrDeviceLimitReached the deviceId stays cached, so the next request hits the cache early-return and authenticates successfully, making limit enforcement one-shot and inconsistent.

WHAT: ProvideAnonDBStore now requires a bare int64 deviceLimit but pkg/server/wire.go still lists it as a provider with no int64 binding. WHY: Wire cannot resolve the bare int64 dependency (only construction site passing cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is manual in impl.go), so generation/build breaks or creates a duplicate store with divergent limits.

WHAT: Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget tagging (background context with 2m timeout) to synchronous TagDevice doing CountDevices + upsert inline. WHY: Every anonymous-request cache miss now pays two DB round-trips on the auth hot path, adding latency and DB fanout under load versus the prior async path.

TOCTOU race: count is checked then a new device is inserted in separate DB round-trips with no lock/transaction. Two concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls for different new device_ids can both see count < deviceLimit and both insert, exceeding the limit and breaking the size invariant this PR adds.

issues.descricao: The device limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate non-atomic steps, so concurrent requests from new devices can all pass the check and exceed the configured limit.
issues.textoGolden: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

comentarios.texto: The limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate steps with no lock or transaction. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Make the count-and-insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit.

The device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by an insert. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the number of devices exceeds deviceLimit. Make the check and insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit, or serialize the check and insert under a lock.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice does check-then-act (CountDevices then INSERT/UPSERT) with no lock, transaction, or unique-guard when deviceLimit>0. WHY: Two concurrent new-device requests can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit and breaking the enforcement contract. HOW: Enforce atomically (e.g., conditional insert guarded by count in one statement/transaction with serializable lock, or re-check count on conflict).

issues.descricao: Device slots are keyed by the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no validation or rate limiting, so an anonymous caller can fill the limit with fake IDs and deny anonymous access to every new legitimate device.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Device slots counted toward deviceLimit are keyed by the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header (read in impl.go TagDevice) with no validation or rate-limit. WHY: Any anonymous caller can mint arbitrary device IDs to fill the table up to the limit, after which all legitimate new anonymous devices get ErrDeviceLimitReached and authentication is denied — a trivial anonymous-access DoS introduced by the limit. HOW: Do not let a single client consume many slots (e.g., bind slot consumption to IP/fingerprint, rate-limit new-device creation, or require proof of distinct device).

issues.descricao: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit and never verifies that an existing device can still be updated at the limit.

comentarios.texto: The at-limit call reuses a brand-new device ID ("keep") that was never inserted, so it only reaches updateDevice's `rowsAffected == 0` -> ErrDeviceLimitReached branch. The success branch of the newly added updateDevice (an existing device still being updated while the store is at the limit) is never exercised by any test — every other call uses deviceLimit 0, so updateDevice is never invoked. A regression that made updateDevice always affect 0 rows, use a wrong WHERE/SET, or unconditionally return ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever limit>0 would leave this and all other tests green. Add a case that, after the store is at the limit, calls CreateOrUpdateDevice again with the SAME DeviceID and asserts require.NoError (and ideally that client_ip/user_agent/updated_at were changed), so the update path is actually verified.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It would still pass if updateDevice always returned ErrDeviceLimitReached, because it never re-submits the existing device (DeviceID "32mdo31deeqwes") at the limit. Add a call that updates the existing device with a new UserAgent or UpdatedAt, require NoError, and check the stored row changed.

issues.descricao: tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice; when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry stays, so the next request from the same device skips the limit check and authenticates for up to 29 minutes.
issues.textoGolden: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TagDevice failures that triggered the new ErrDeviceLimitReached early-return are not permanent, because tagDeviceUI (impl.go:87) writes the device key into localCache BEFORE CreateOrUpdateDevice (impl.go:93) and never evicts it on error; tagDeviceUI returns early on any cache hit (impl.go:83-84). WHY: the first request from a new over-limit device is denied, but the poisoned cache makes every subsequent request from that same device skip the limit check entirely and authenticate successfully, so the configurable device limit is bypassed by simply retrying. HOW: only set the cache key after CreateOrUpdateDevice returns nil (e.g. move a.localCache.SetDefault after the successful DB write, or delete the key when it returns ErrDeviceLimitReached).

TagDevice now propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached to deny an over-limit anonymous device, but tagDeviceUI (impl.go:83-95) records the device in localCache at line 87 *before* calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects the device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached, so the next request for that same device returns early at line 83 with a nil error and the device is admitted. The limit therefore only blocks the first request and is silently bypassed on retry. Fix by only setting the cache entry after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (move SetDefault after the store call), or by removing/not caching the key on failure.

The new authentication gate accepts retries from devices that were rejected by the limit because tagDeviceUI inserts the cache entry before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. At capacity, the first request with a new X-Grafana-Device-Id fails, but subsequent requests with that same ID hit the 29-minute cache and receive an anonymous identity without admission to the device store. Cache only successful admissions, and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful.

issues.descricao: Device tagging now runs synchronously in Authenticate, adding DB round-trips on cache-miss anonymous requests where it used to be fire-and-forget.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Anonymous.Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget goroutine TagDevice to synchronous TagDevice(ctx) that runs CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE inline. WHY: Every cache-miss anonymous authentication now blocks on two DB round-trips in the login hot path, adding latency and DB load per request where previously auth returned immediately. HOW: Restore async tagging for the non-limit path or at least decouple denial from the hot path (e.g., async count with cached count, or only synchronously enforce when near limit).

issues.descricao: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting has no entry in conf/defaults.ini, so the GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT environment override is ignored and the limit stays 0.

comentarios.texto: The new device_limit setting is read without adding a corresponding key to conf/defaults.ini. applyEnvVariableOverrides only visits keys already present in the loaded INI and runs before readAuthSettings, so setting GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT alone is ignored and leaves the limit at zero, disabling enforcement. Add an uncommented device_limit = 0 entry under auth.anonymous in defaults.ini so the standard environment override mechanism can apply it.

issues.descricao: The anonymous device limit is enforced only through TagDevice, which returns nil when the client-controlled device ID header is missing, so requests without the header authenticate anonymously regardless of the configured limit.

The doc comment on updateDevice says it updates a device "updated between the given times", but the function takes no times, computes the 30-day window itself and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when no row matches.
updateDevice prepends the query to the captured args inside the retried DB callback, so a SQLite lock retry runs Exec with the query duplicated in the arguments and the update fails.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive entryPointAssetsCacheMu and holds it across readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN IO with no second cache check after Lock. WHY: N concurrent cold-start (or every Dev-mode) requests serialize on the write lock and each performs redundant file/CDN reads while blocking all RLock readers. HOW: Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and return early on hit, and ideally do the file/CDN load outside the lock then re-lock only to publish.

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that missed the cache each reload the assets manifest.
issues.textoGolden: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.
cache is not re-checked under the lock after re-acquiring write Lock, so concurrent callers can each recompute web assets

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets holds a global exclusive mutex through the whole manifest load, so in Dev mode, where the cache is bypassed, every request serializes behind it.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware and mutates its next field on every CreateClientMiddleware call instead of returning a new instance. WHY: The middlewares slice is reused to build many decorator chains so concurrent/sequential builds overwrite imw.next causing wrong delegation and a data race. HOW: Return a new wrapper per call like ContextualLoggerMiddleware does, e.g. copy the struct and set next on the copy.

WHAT: QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics dereference req.PluginContext without the nil-req guard that LoggerMiddleware has. WHY: A nil request panics the backend plugin path instead of delegating to next. HOW: Add the same if req == nil { return m.next.X(ctx, req) } guard to each method.

WHAT: QueryData ranges over req.Queries and CallResource reads len(req.Body) without nil-req guards. WHY: A nil request panics where LoggerMiddleware explicitly delegates nil requests to next. HOW: Add if req == nil { return m.next.X(...) } guards matching LoggerMiddleware.

WHAT: instrumentPluginRequestSize/instrumentPluginRequest return plugins.ErrPluginNotRegistered when the plugin is missing from the registry and callers return before invoking next. WHY: An observability lookup failure fails the functional plugin request (QueryData returns nil plus error) instead of best-effort metrics. HOW: Log the target-lookup error and still call next instead of returning early.

WHAT: LoggerMiddleware removed explicit pluginId, endpoint, dsName/dsUID, uname and traceID fields and relies solely on FromContext, but instrumentContext never adds traceID. WHY: Plugin Request Completed logs lose traceID correlation (and all fields when Logger is used without Contextual middleware first). HOW: Re-add traceID via tracing.TraceIDFromContext or make instrumentContext include it.

WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger instead of the receiver. WHY: LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info so assertions on the injected fake never see the call and counts/messages are lost. HOW: Return f (or a wrapper sharing the same Logs pointers) instead of a new instance.

HELP text says 'returned' implying response size, but instrumentPluginRequestSize observes inbound sizes (len(Query.JSON), len(CallResource Body)). Users reading Prometheus HELP will misinterpret the metric. Remove 'returned'.

File and constructor were renamed NewInstrumentationMiddleware -> NewMetricsMiddleware/metrics_middleware.go, but test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. Stale name misdescribes what is tested and confuses navigation.

Missing nil-request guard causes panic: QueryData dereferences req.Queries, CallResource dereferences req.Body, CheckHealth/CollectMetrics dereference req.PluginContext. LoggerMiddleware in the same chain guards req==nil, proving nil is reachable. Add if req==nil passthrough before instrumenting, matching LoggerMiddleware.

Missing nil-request guard causes panic: all four methods dereference req.PluginContext via instrumentContext without checking req==nil. LoggerMiddleware guards this case so nil reaches the chain. Add if req==nil passthrough to next before calling instrumentContext in QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics.

Fake violates Logger.FromContext contract (ifaces.go: has this logger's context plus given context) by returning a fresh unrelated logger. LoggerMiddleware calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so with TestLogger the log goes to a new instance and is unobservable/loses base context. Return the receiver (or a copy preserving it) instead.

logger_middleware.go removed explicit traceID log param assuming FromContext supplies it, but instrumentContext only adds endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname and never propagates tracing.TraceIDFromContext. Trace correlation in Plugin Request Completed logs is lost. Propagate traceID into WithContextualAttributes or retain explicit logging.

Incorrect measurement: float64(elapsed/time.Millisecond) divides Durations as int64 nanoseconds first, truncating sub-millisecond fractions to 0 and all other values down to whole ms. Buckets start at 0.005ms so precision matters, and the seconds histogram on the same request uses precise elapsed.Seconds(). Convert first: float64(elapsed)/float64(time.Millisecond). Applies to both Observe and ObserveWithExemplar paths.

Logic error: foundLabels is declared outside the per-metric loop and never reset, so counts accumulate across series; combined with returning an error on the first label-value mismatch instead of skipping that series, a family with more than one series will miscount or falsely fail. Reset the counter per metric and skip non-matching series.

The shouldInstrumentRequestSize=false cases (CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) are never asserted: the if at line 101 has no else, so if those endpoints incorrectly started emitting grafana_plugin_request_size_bytes the test would still pass. Add an else asserting CollectAndCount(metricRequestSize)==0.

issues.descricao: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger instead of the receiver, so logs written via the contextual logger are lost to assertions on the original fake.
issues.textoGolden: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger instead of the receiver. WHY: LoggerMiddleware calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info so the write goes to a throwaway instance and assertions on the original TestLogger Calls/Message never observe it, diverging from real wrapper that preserves logger context. HOW: Return f (or a child sharing f) instead of NewTestLogger.

issues.descricao: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after the middleware was renamed to MetricsMiddleware.

comentarios.texto: TestInstrumentationMiddleware still carries the old name even though this PR renamed the middleware under test to MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware/NewMetricsMiddleware) and the file to metrics_middleware_test.go. The identifier advertises the superseded "InstrumentationMiddleware" name; rename it (e.g. TestMetricsMiddleware) so the test name matches the code it exercises.
Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware but it constructs and asserts MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware). Rename to TestMetricsMiddleware to match the renamed middleware.

issues.descricao: The FromContext doc comment is copied from New() and misdescribes the method, which attaches attributes stored in the context.Context.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: All four async legacy writes derive the timeout context from the request ctx, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns. WHY: The child context is immediately cancelled so the fire-and-forget legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection never completes, defeating mode-3 safety write. HOW: Derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background() with the 10s timeout instead of the cancellable request ctx (same fix at Delete:110, Update:135, DeleteCollection:163).

WHAT: Create (and Update:129) call recordLegacyDuration with startStorage when Storage.Create/Update fails. WHY: Storage failures are attributed to the legacy histogram and storage failures become invisible, breaking alerts/dashboards. HOW: Call recordStorageDuration on the storage error paths.

WHAT: The async legacy DeleteCollection path calls recordStorageDuration with startLegacy. WHY: Legacy latency/errors pollute the storage histogram and legacy SLIs are never observed. HOW: Call recordLegacyDuration for the legacy measurement.

WHAT: Delete success path passes name (unbounded object name) as the kind label where every other call passes options.Kind. WHY: Each distinct object creates a new Prometheus series, causing unbounded cardinality, memory blowup and slow queries. HOW: Pass options.Kind like the error path on line 103 does.

WHAT: Delete builds an enriched log with name/kind/method but propagates d.Log into the context instead of log. WHY: Downstream Storage/Delete and the async legacy goroutine lose name/kind/method fields, breaking log correlation added by this PR. HOW: Propagate log as every other method does.

WHAT: The old code computed UpdatedObject once and reused it for both stores via updateWrapper; the new code passes the same objInfo to Storage.Update and then Legacy.Update, invoking UpdatedObject twice on different old objects. WHY: Non-idempotent UpdatedObject funcs (timestamps, defaults, resourceVersion) produce divergent unified vs legacy objects and the async invocation races with caller reuse of objInfo/options. HOW: Compute once and fan out the same updated payload, or deep-copy inputs before the goroutine.

Background Legacy write derives context from request ctx; when handler returns the ctx is cancelled so 10s timeout child is immediately cancelled and legacy write lost, diverging stores. Detach with WithoutCancel/Background. Same in Delete/Update/DeleteCollection goroutines.

Same obj pointer returned as created and read concurrently by background goroutine (likewise objInfo/options in Update); Storage impls mutate in place -> data race / torn legacy write. Deep-copy before handing to goroutine.

Create returns before the go-func legacy Create runs, but the test asserts only the storage result and never verifies the legacy mock was called. Removing d.Legacy.Create would still pass. Wait on the async effect (e.g. Eventually + AssertCalled) before asserting.

Delete legacy write is async, but test sets up only Storage mock and asserts only storage return. Deleting the legacy-delete goroutine would still pass. Register legacy Delete expectation and wait/assert it was called.

Update legacy write is in goroutine and mock expectation is registered with m.On but never asserted, with no wait. Removing legacy Update would still pass. Add Eventually/AssertCalled for legacy Update.

DeleteCollection legacy path is async but test only mocks/asserts Storage and returns immediately. Breaking or removing legacy DeleteCollection goroutine would still pass. Register and wait/assert the legacy call.

Success path records storage duration with `name` where the kind label is expected (error path above uses options.Kind and legacy path below uses options.Kind). The series will be untaggable/unjoinable with the other mode-3 series. Use options.Kind.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded via recordStorageDuration while Create/Delete/Update legacy paths use recordLegacyDuration. Legacy latency will inflate/deflate the storage histogram and leave the legacy histogram empty. Use recordLegacyDuration.

Delete computes enriched `log` but derives the context from `d.Log`, discarding name/kind/method fields; every other method (Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection) passes `log`. Downstream storage calls lose the fields. Pass `log`.

Storage Create error path calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time while the success path calls recordStorageDuration. Failures will pollute the legacy histogram and hide storage errors. Use recordStorageDuration on the storage error path (Update has the identical swap at line 129).

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: DualWriterMode3.Delete now returns on any unified-storage error, including NotFound, before deleting from legacy, so objects that exist only in legacy can no longer be deleted.
Mode 3 legacy-storage write errors (create/update/delete/delete-collection) are no longer logged after moving to async goroutines; only a duration metric with an error flag is recorded.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Removing the whole-function cacheMu lock leaves only the final map write locked, so two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource both run bleve.New/list/build simultaneously. WHY: For file-backed indexes both create the same dir (filepath.Join Root/namespace/resource.group), causing lock contention/corruption, leaked index handles, double IndexTenants.Inc, and last-writer-wins cache churn when init errgroup and Search-triggered getOrCreateIndex race. HOW: Deduplicate same-key builds with per-key singleflight/locking while keeping cross-key parallelism.

WHAT: initWatcher was moved to run after the lengthy search.init, so the broadcaster captures its since-RV only after indexing finishes. WHY: Writes committed during index building are invisible to Watch clients (gap in broadcast stream) whereas starting the watcher first buffered/replayed them; it also delays serving watches by the full index duration. HOW: Restore watcher-before-index order or capture the since-RV before indexing and replay deltas after.

WHAT: NewResourceServer creates a cancellable watcher context (ctx,cancel) then returns nil,err on Init failure without calling cancel or stopping already-started search watch goroutines. WHY: Leaks context resources and leaves the search.init WatchWriteEvents background loop running after the server is discarded, holding DB pollers open. HOW: Call cancel() (and stop any partially-initialized components) on the Init error path.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

issues.descricao: The new startup log calls TotalDocs, which iterates the index cache without a lock, after the event goroutine that can add indexes has started, so a concurrent map read and write can crash the process.
issues.textoGolden: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

issues.descricao: NewResourceServer returns an error when Init fails without cancelling the server context created earlier.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.

issues.descricao: The PR skips the storage-server module integration test on postgres instead of fixing the failure, removing coverage of the new eager initialization on postgres.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while sibling branches pass key. WHY: Causes React reconciliation warnings and state/action reuse across rows when the filtered list changes. HOW: Restore key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem.

WHAT: canPause can become true via grafana promRule ability while Pause menu item still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule). WHY: In ruler-free list view rulerRule is undefined so Pause never renders despite allowed ability — dead action path. HOW: Gate Pause item on (rulerRule or promRule) Grafana rule, or pass promRule-derived pause handler.

WHAT: Silence ability is now grantable via promRule alone, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only renders when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) holds. WHY: Clicking Silence on prom-only rows sets showSilenceDrawer with no drawer rendered — silent no-op. HOW: Render drawer from promRule when ruler rule absent or hide Silence when no rulerRule available.

WHAT: Loader now maps only promResponse rules and dropped matchRules Creating/Deleting handling. WHY: Transient deleting rules (prom-only) render as normal rows with full Edit/More actions instead of Deleting state without actions, and creating rules vanish. HOW: Restore operation-aware rendering for prom-only rows or filter/suppress actions while ruler/prom diverge.

Doc block still says the loader loads from 'Prometheus and Ruler endpoints' but this PR removed the Ruler query (useGetGrafanaRulerGroupQuery/matchRules) so it now loads only from Prometheus. Update the comment to describe Prometheus-only loading to avoid misleading callers.
Optional chain stops at .rules, so empty groups yields undefined.map() throw. Default to empty array: (groups.at(0)?.rules ?? []).map(...).
Test named 'with action menu options' never clicks More nor asserts menuitems; it passes even if dropdown is empty/broken. Click More and assert menu items or rename to cover only the button.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) on the skipToken path leaves duplicateSupported=AlwaysSupported with allowed=grafana create permission, so useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) returns [true,true] for Duplicate and AlertRuleMenu ORs ruler||grafana to true for cloud rules that should be gated only by ruler abilities.

Comment states location is redundant in folder>group hierarchy but no showLocation={false} is passed and GrafanaRuleListItem defaults to true, so grouped rules show location contrary to declared intent.

issues.descricao: The pause menu item is still gated on a Grafana ruler rule, but the list view now passes only the Prometheus rule, so Pause/Resume disappears for list-view rules even when the user may pause them.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based pause ability cannot display Pause or Resume for list-view rules because the menu still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) before rendering MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, so these actions disappear even for editable rules. Adapt the pause menu item to accept the Grafana identifier and Prometheus pause state, or load the ruler rule on demand.

issues.descricao: The Delete menu item still requires a ruler rule, which list-view Grafana rules no longer provide, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based delete ability is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule` when rendering the Delete item. Both Grafana list-view paths now omit rulerRule, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely. Render deletion using the available identifier and group identifier instead of requiring the ruler DTO, adapting the callback contract accordingly.

issues.descricao: When the Grafana prom-rule branch is skipped (datasource rules), useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still reports Duplicate as supported and allowed by Grafana create permission, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler ability, so Duplicate appears on cloud rules even when the ruler check denies it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: canDuplicate ORs ruler ability with grafana ability where grafana path is skipToken=>undefined for cloud rules, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate=[true,true] whenever the user has global Grafana create permission. WHY: Any user with Grafana rule-create gets Duplicate menu item on cloud/Mimir rules even when ruler abilities deny it — incorrect authorization gating. HOW: Return NotSupported for all abilities when rule is skipToken/undefined, or gate grafana branch on prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) before ORing.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities returns AlwaysSupported for Duplicate when rule is undefined (skipToken): loading is false from the !rule early-return, so MaybeSupported=true and duplicateSupported=true. ORed in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons this leaks Grafana create permission into non-Grafana rules. Gate MaybeSupported/duplicateSupported on rule existence (e.g. NotSupported when !rule).

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities must return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined (skipToken). Currently MaybeSupported falls back to AlwaysSupported when !loading, so Duplicate=[true, global-create] is true for a cloud rule passed as skipToken, and AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons OR-logic then incorrectly enables Duplicate (and Explore). Guard with if (!rule) return all-NotSupported abilities or make MaybeSupported require rule.

issues.descricao: The refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities into useAllRulerRuleAbilities drops the isFederatedRuleGroup check (isFederated is hardcoded false), so federated Mimir rules are reported as editable and deletable.

comentarios.texto: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, so federated Mimir rules are no longer treated as immutable and can show edit and delete abilities. Keep the federation check in this wrapper, or pass the federation state into the shared hook.

Delegating useAllAlertRuleAbilities to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group's federation status and replaces the previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check with a constant false. Legacy RuleActionsButtons consequently enables editing rules in groups with source_tenants, although these groups were explicitly immutable before this change. Preserve the CombinedRule federation check in the wrapper or pass federation status into the delegated ability calculation.

Preserve the federated-group immutability check when delegating this CombinedRule hook. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities inspected rule.group with isFederatedRuleGroup and disabled modification/removal for federated rules. The replacement delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated=false and receives no group information. Existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities consumers therefore now receive supported update/delete abilities for federated rules when datasource permissions allow them, exposing operations that the previous contract explicitly prohibited. Pass the federation state through or retain that restriction in this wrapper.

issues.descricao: The Grafana prom-rule abilities gate Pause, Restore, Export and DeletePermanently on alertingRule(rule) while the comment claims it checks Grafana-managed rules, so Grafana recording rules lose these actions in the list view.

comentarios.texto: The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the variable it describes is `isAlertingRule`. That variable is true only for alerting rules and false for Grafana recording rules. Fix the comment, or rename the variable, so it says the check is for alerting rules. As written, readers will expect Pause, Export and Silence to be enabled for recording rules.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the check used is alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. Pause, Restore, ModifyExport and DeletePermanently are therefore wrongly disabled for Grafana recording rules, where the old isGrafanaManagedAlertRule check allowed them. Use prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule) for these abilities, and keep alertingRule only for Silence.

issues.descricao: The comment claims GrafanaPromRuleDTO abilities have no loading state, but the next line makes support depend on the folder loading flag.

comentarios.texto: The comment says there is no loading state, but the next line is `loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`. `loading` comes from the folder fetch. Update the comment to say that support depends on the folder loading state.

issues.descricao: The Grafana branch of the filtered rule list renders GrafanaRuleListItem without a key prop, so React reconciles the streaming list by index and warns about missing keys.
issues.textoGolden: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The grafana branch of the filtered list renders <GrafanaRuleListItem .../> without a `key` prop, dropping the `key={key}` that the replaced <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../> had. WHY: `rules.map` renders a dynamic list keyed by getRuleKey/hashRule; without a key React logs duplicate-key warnings and reconciles rows by index, so as the async rule stream updates/reorders the wrong rule row can be reused/mutated (stale state, swapped actions). HOW: add `key={key}` (the value is already destructured on line 152) to the <GrafanaRuleListItem> element.

WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while datasource and unknown branches pass key. WHY: Breaks React list reconciliation — wrong item reuse, stale actions/state and console key warnings for every Grafana hit. HOW: Add key={key} to the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

issues.descricao: The test named 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks the More button exists, never the menu options.

comentarios.texto: The test 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks that the More button exists. It finds the button by name 'More', so the aria-label and text assertions are tautological. It would pass even if the menu had no actions or the abilities were broken. Click the button and assert the expected menu items, or rename the test to match what it checks.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never verifies any action menu option: the body only asserts the More button exists and has aria-label/text 'More'. It would still pass if the dropdown were rendered empty (Silence/Duplicate/Copy link/Export all missing), i.e. the behaviour the name promises is not covered. Either open the menu and assert the menu items, or rename the test to reflect that it only checks the trigger button's rendering/accessibility.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu nor asserts menu items — it only checks More button presence/aria/text. Click More and assert expected menuitems (or rename to 'should render More button') so it fails if menu actions break.

issues.descricao: GrafanaGroupLoader's JSDoc still says it loads from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints after the ruler query was removed.

comentarios.texto: The JSDoc for GrafanaGroupLoader still says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints." but this PR removed the ruler API query entirely — the component now only calls useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery (Prometheus). The documentation describes a data source the function no longer consumes; update it to state only the Prometheus endpoint is loaded (and the same stale "Ruler response" reference in the expectedRulesCount prop doc at lines 18–19 should be corrected).

issues.descricao: For list-view Grafana rules RuleActionsButtons gets only promRule, so the Silence menu item is shown but the silence drawer, still gated on a ruler alerting rule, never renders and clicking Silence does nothing.
issues.textoGolden: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

comentarios.texto: Passing only promRule enables the Silence notifications menu item but leaves RuleActionsButtons.V2 unable to render its silence drawer, which is guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Clicking Silence only updates showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing because rule is undefined. Update the drawer to accept a rule UID—the inspected SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only needs grafana_alert.uid—and allow the Prometheus alerting-rule path to render it.

The new list item passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but that component renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only under `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. With rule undefined, clicking the newly enabled 'Silence notifications' action only sets state and never opens a drawer. Adapt the silence rendering path to load/use the rule by its Prometheus identifier before switching this caller to promRule-only.

WHAT: getEditableIdentifier now enables a prom-only path (Grafana uid identifier with rulerRule undefined) but the silence drawer still renders only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. WHY: In the list view Silence menu item can be shown via grafana abilities, clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer but the drawer never mounts, so Silence silently does nothing. HOW: Gate the drawer on promRule as well or provide a prom-based silence drawer.

issues.descricao: RulesTable RBAC tests only mock useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities and leave useRulerRuleAbilities denied, so the ruler-based Delete permission branch of AlertRuleMenu is never tested.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Constructor calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType,...) twice and never checks rawTokenId. WHY: Null rawTokenId passes validation and later produces "null" suffix or NPE in encodeTokenId/getTokenContextFromTokenId. HOW: Change second check to Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed").

WHAT: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory adds abstract String getShortcut() with no default implementation. WHY: Every existing third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory fails to compile and already-deployed ones throw AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls getShortcut(), breaking server startup/token issuance. HOW: Provide a default method (e.g. default returning getId() or a derived value) instead of abstract.

WHAT: isAccessTokenId uses substring(3,5) instead of (4,6) and returns false when the shortcut equals the expectation. WHY: Matcher rejects correct token IDs and accepts wrong-grant IDs, so grant-encoding assertions pass/fail inverted and mask regressions. HOW: Negate the equality and slice the last 2 chars of the 6-char prefix (substring(4,6)).

WHAT: grantType is snapshotted in the constructor but setFormParams() replaces formParams without updating it, and constructor NPEs on null formParams. WHY: Any path mutating form params leaves context.getGrantType() stale so OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse stores the wrong grant into the token ID; null params now crash where previously tolerated. HOW: Sync grantType in setFormParams() and null-guard the constructor lookup (or compute lazily from formParams).

WHAT: initToken unconditionally encodes the ID and encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException for any grantType with no registered shortcut. WHY: Custom/extension grants or any flow setting an unmapped grant string turn previously-successful token issuance into a 500 error. HOW: Fall back to rawTokenId (or UNKNOWN shortcut) when no shortcut is mapped instead of throwing.
Second requireNonNull checks grantType again while its message says rawTokenId, so null rawTokenId slips through and the message disagrees with the code. Check rawTokenId instead.
Doc says 3-letters shortcut yet every grant factory in this PR returns 2 chars (ac, rt, ci, dg, cc, pg, pc, ro, te, na). Fix doc to 2-letters to match the code.
Logic is inverted: `if (equals) return false` fails when the grant matches and passes when it mismatches. Negate the condition so mismatch returns false.

Cross-reference mismatch with encoder: encode is session(0,2)+token(2,4)+grant(4,6) and decode uses substring(4,6) for grant, but matcher reads substring(3,5). Use substring(4,6) to agree with DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.
Copy-paste error: second requireNonNull checks grantType again instead of rawTokenId, so null rawTokenId is never rejected. Check rawTokenId.

Generator encodes 2-char session + 2-char token + 2-char grant (grant at index 4-6) but validator reads substring(3,5) and returns false when equal. Fix to !substring(4,6).equals(...) so mismatched grants are rejected and matching grants pass.
Comparison is inverted: it returns false (rejects) when the extracted shortcut equals the expected grant, and accepts otherwise. Negate the condition so mismatched grants are rejected.

Encoded prefix is session(0,2)+tokenType(2,4)+grant(4,6) per encoder/decoder, but matcher extracts substring(3,5) (second char of tokenType + first char of grant). Use substring(4,6); e.g. 'onrtna' grant 'na' is at 4,6 not 3,5.

matchesSafely is inverted and slices the wrong chars: it returns false when the grant shortcut equals expected, and checks substring(3,5) instead of the grant at substring(4,6). Result: any UUID passes regardless of grant, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/etc would still pass if the wrong grant were encoded.
Second requireNonNull checks grantType instead of rawTokenId, so null rawTokenId creates invalid context and later encode corruption. Fix to requireNonNull(rawTokenId).

Grant shortcut occupies chars 4-6 of 6-char prefix but code checks substring(3,5) and returns false when equal, so correct IDs fail and wrong IDs pass; also needs length guard to avoid StringIndexOutOfBounds.

issues.descricao: The AccessTokenContext constructor checks grantType twice instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation and is encoded as ':null'.
issues.textoGolden: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the constructor validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId` (`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`). WHY: a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted, so `encodeTokenId` produces a token id ending in `:null` and any later consumer of the raw id gets an invalid value instead of an early failure. HOW: change the argument to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

Line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") — it validates grantType a second time (line 72 already does) with a message naming a different field. rawTokenId is never validated, so a null rawTokenId is accepted at construction and the advertised check/message is wrong. It should be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed").

The null-check message names the wrong parameter: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` validates `grantType` but reports `rawTokenId`, and it duplicates the check on line 72 while `rawTokenId` is never validated at all. The message that reaches the reader contradicts the code it guards; it should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

issues.descricao: isAccessTokenId reads the grant shortcut at the wrong offset (3,5 instead of 4,6) and inverts the comparison, so the event assertions never verify the token's grant type.
issues.textoGolden: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `isAccessTokenId` reads the grant shortcut from the wrong offset and inverts the comparison — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. WHY: for the encoded id `ssttgg:raw` the grant shortcut occupies 0-based indices 4-5, so `substring(3,5)` inspects the token-type/grant boundary and can never equal the expected shortcut; combined with the inverted `return false`, the equality branch is unreachable and the matcher validates only the UUID part. As a result the new assertions in `expectCodeToToken`/`expectRefresh`/`expectDeviceCodeToToken`/`expectAuthReqIdToToken` do not actually assert the grant type and would pass even if the grant shortcut were wrong. HOW: use `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and negate the condition (`if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`).

The matcher logic is inverted: line 483 returns false when the extracted grant shortcut EQUALS expectedGrantShortcut, so a token that actually carries the expected grant fails the matcher, while a token with any other grant shortcut falls through and passes. The condition should be negated: `if (!items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Also note the encode site writes the grant shortcut at chars 4-6 (substring(4,6)); substring(3,5) reads one character early into the token-type field, so the offset is off by one relative to TokenManager.encodeTokenId.

The comment 'Grant type shortcut starts at character 4th char' disagrees with the encoding that this PR defines (sessionType chars 1-2, tokenType 3-4, grantType 5-6, e.g. 'trltcc'), and the code reads substring(3,5) — the 4th-5th chars, i.e. the token-type second char plus the grant first char, never the grant shortcut. The comment (and the index) should point at the 5th char / substring(4,6).

issues.descricao: getShortcut() Javadoc says shortcuts are usually 3 letters, but the encoding requires exactly 2-character shortcuts.
issues.textoGolden: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc says getShortcut() returns 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', but every implementation introduced in this PR returns a 2-character shortcut ('ac','cc','pg','pc','rt','ro','te','ci','dg') and the encoder relies on exactly 2 chars (encoded context length 6 = 2+2+2). The doc states a length the code does not produce; it should say 2-character shortcut.

Grant shortcuts are registered without enforcing the two-character length required by the decoder. A custom grant returning a three-character shortcut, which the new OAuth2GrantTypeFactory documentation explicitly suggests, produces a seven-character prefix that getTokenContextFromTokenId rejects, breaking encode/decode round trips for that grant. Validate shortcut length during registration and dynamic refresh, and document the required two-character format.

The new contract describes getShortcut() as usually returning a three-letter shortcut, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider requires exactly two characters for the grant field (six total prefix characters, decoded with substring(4, 6)). An extension author following this documentation can produce token IDs that the default decoder rejects. Document the required two-character length rather than advertising three letters.

issues.descricao: testIncorrectGrantType catches any RuntimeException, so it passes on a NullPointerException from the unset sessionFactory rather than verifying the unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException.
issues.textoGolden: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

comentarios.texto: Catching RuntimeException allows this negative test to pass for an unrelated fixture failure. The fixture constructs the factory without postInit, leaving sessionFactory null; resolving the unregistered `ac` shortcut calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream and throws NullPointerException before the decoder's intended unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException. Catch/assert IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a factory fixture whose lookup returns no matching grant, so removing the decoder's validation would fail the test.

issues.descricao: Client-credentials (and UMA permission) token issuance never sets the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so their access token ids are encoded with the unknown grant 'na' instead of their shortcut.

comentarios.texto: The new grant metadata falls back to 'na' for client-credentials and UMA tokens because their issuance paths never set Constants.GRANT_TYPE on their fresh ClientSessionContext. ClientCredentialsGrantType calls responseBuilder.generateAccessToken directly, and PermissionGrantType delegates to AuthorizationTokenService, so neither executes the new assignment in createTokenResponse; tokens from these known grants therefore carry unknown grant context. Set the grant attribute in both issuance paths before generating the access token.

issues.descricao: Lazy registration of newly deployed grants does not check shortcut uniqueness, so a grant reusing an existing shortcut silently overwrites the reverse mapping and older tokens decode to the wrong grant.

comentarios.texto: Enforce shortcut uniqueness during lazy registration rather than overwriting grantsByShortcuts. If a newly deployed grant B uses existing grant A's shortcut, this path replaces shortcut→A with shortcut→B while retaining both forward entries. Previously issued A tokens then decode as B. Concurrent registrations of two new grants with the same shortcut likewise both succeed, with the last inverse-map write winning. Use collision-aware atomic registration and reject the conflicting grant before publishing its forward mapping.

issues.descricao: getShortcut() is added as an abstract method to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without a default, breaking existing custom grant type factories (compile error or AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls it).

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Changed getSubGroupsCount returns null when the group was concurrently deleted. WHY: It violates GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount contract documented as Never returns null, shifting the NPE to any caller that unboxes or assumes non-null instead of fixing the race. HOW: Return a non-null fallback (e.g. 0L) or delegate to invalidation path consistent with getSubGroupsStream handling.

WHAT: Reader thread is started but never joined before asserting caughtExceptions is empty. WHY: The assertion can run while requests are still in-flight (missed failures/flaky) and the spinning thread leaks past the test, hammering the server during subsequent tests.
