comentarios.texto: WHAT: website_name re-exposes the user's website for profiles where it is intentionally hidden — the attribute is added to the public `attributes` list (line 43) but not to `untrusted_attributes`, and `include_website_name` only checks `website.present?` instead of `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. WHY: `website` is an untrusted attribute gated by `restrict_user_fields?` (lib/guardian/user_guardian.rb:58-60), which is true for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor; `website_name` derives `website_host + path` from the same `object.user_profile.website`, so the URL that `include_website?` suppresses is still disclosed through the new key (the existing spec at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11-14 only asserts the listed untrusted keys are absent, so this leak is not covered). HOW: add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or have `include_website_name` return false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`), mirroring the `website` handling.

`website_name` is derived from the same `object.user_profile.website` value that `:website` protects via `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), but it is only gated by `include_website_name` -> `website.present?`. Since the untrusted filter removes `website` for some viewers while `website_name` is still emitted, and in the same-domain / subdomain branches it returns host *plus* `URI(website).path` (lines 143/146/149), the user's full website URL still leaves in the response for viewers the filter was supposed to strip it from. Either add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` or gate `include_website_name` with the same trust condition as `website`.

The new `website_name` field is gated only on `website.present?`, ignoring the visibility constraint this file declares for its source attribute: lines 105-111 put `:website` in `untrusted_attributes`, so `website` is omitted for viewers not allowed to see profile fields, but `website_name` is still serialized because `include_website_name` never consults that condition. Those viewers now receive the user's URL host, and when the host equals (lines 141-143) or is a parent of (144-149) the instance host they receive host + path, i.e. the complete URL that `website` was supposed to hide. Fix by adding `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (105-111) — or make the guard reuse `website`'s own inclusion condition instead of a bare presence check.

issues.descricao: include_website_name lacks the '?' suffix that ActiveModelSerializers requires, so the conditional-inclusion guard is never called.
issues.textoGolden: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` required by ActiveModelSerializers. WHY: every other conditional-inclusion guard in this file uses the `?` form (`define_method "include_#{attr}?"` at lines 9/18/27, `include_email?` at line 117), and AMS 0.8.3 resolves the guard as `include_<attr>?`; because this method lacks the `?` it is never invoked, so the intended `website.present?` condition is silently ignored and `website_name` is always serialized. HOW: rename to `def include_website_name?`.

The guard method is named `include_website_name`, but ActiveModelSerializers (and this file's own convention, e.g. `include_email?` at line 117) resolves per-attribute guards via `include_<attribute>?`. Because the name lacks the trailing `?`, the framework never invokes it: the `website.present?` guard is dead code and `website_name` is serialized unconditionally, emitting `website_name: null` for users without a website. Rename to `include_website_name?`.

The conditional-inclusion guard is named `include_website_name`, but ActiveModelSerializers resolves these guards as `include_<attribute>?` (the sibling in this very file is `include_email?` at line 117). As written the method is never called, so the guard is dead and the `:website_name` attribute declared at line 43 is serialized unconditionally. That defeats the intent of the guard (`website.present?`): the payload now always carries `website_name`, including for the scopes where `website` itself is withheld by the `untrusted_attributes` list (line 109), leaking the user's site host/path to viewers who were never meant to receive the website. Rename the method to `include_website_name?` so the serializer base class honors it.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: runSplitQuery re-applies applyTemplateVariables to queries already interpolated by runShardSplitQuery. WHY: subRequest at shardQuerySplitting.ts:154 spreads original scopedVars/filters so the second pass re-runs addAdHocFilters, duplicating ad-hoc labels and corrupting the expr sent to runQuery. HOW: skip re-interpolation for already-interpolated targets or clear scopedVars/filters on the delegated subRequest.

WHAT: Switching from interpolateVariablesInQueries to applyTemplateVariables drops the datasource:getRef() assignment. WHY: Old method (datasource.ts:436-438) stamped each query with datasource ref; new method (datasource.ts:1135-1140) returns only expr/step/legendFormat, leaving stale/missing datasource on split targets for downstream routing. HOW: Preserve the datasource ref when mapping, as the old path did.

issues.descricao: Loki split/shard queries are now interpolated with applyTemplateVariables before splitting and again on execution, so ad hoc filters are applied twice and already-substituted values are re-interpolated.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 52), but it then delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery (line 163), which this PR also changed to call datasource.applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299), so each target is interpolated (and ad hoc filters applied) twice. WHY: double interpolation re-runs addAdHocFilters on an already-filtered expression; the stream-selector path masks the duplicate via labelExists() dedup in addFilterToStreamSelector (modifyQuery.ts:494), but parsed/structured-metadata labels use addFilterAsLabelFilter which does not dedup, producing duplicated label filters, and any interpolated value containing '$' can be re-interpolated. This is confirmed by the updated test expecting applyTemplateVariables toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) for a single target (1 call here + 4 sub-requests through runSplitQuery) instead of 1. HOW: interpolate only once — either remove the interpolation added to runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery do it, or have splitQueriesByStreamShard pass the already-interpolated targets without re-interpolating in runSplitQuery.

The newly interpolated targets are interpolated again by DataSourceWithBackend.query when runQuery executes each split request. TemplateSrv.replace scans the resulting string again, so a variable whose literal value contains another defined variable token (for example, a log-search value containing `$other`) is expanded a second time and produces a different query from the non-splitting path; shard splitting also passes through this additional interpolation. Preserve the early interpolation needed for partitioning while ensuring already-interpolated targets are not interpolated again on execution, and test through the real backend query preparation rather than mocking runQuery.

Targets are interpolated here with `applyTemplateVariables`, including ad hoc filters, and then sent to `datasource.runQuery`, which interpolates them again through the backend path (datasource.ts:324/377). The ad hoc filters may be injected twice, and already-substituted values are re-interpolated, which can produce wrong or invalid LogQL. Interpolate only once. Either clear `scopedVars` and `filters` on the sub-requests after the first pass, or skip interpolation in `runQuery` for already-interpolated requests. The same issue applies to shardQuerySplitting.ts:52.

issues.descricao: runShardSplitQuery now filters empty/hidden targets before interpolation, so an expr that interpolates to an empty string is no longer dropped.

comentarios.texto: The order of operations was inverted relative to the previous contract: interpolation used to run before the `expr`/`hide` filters (interpolateVariablesInQueries(targets).filter(...)), and now the filters run on the *raw* targets before `applyTemplateVariables` is applied. Filtering on the un-interpolated `query.expr` means the previous fallback that dropped a target once variable substitution had emptied its expression no longer exists: a target like `{ expr: '$myVar' }` whose variable resolves to '' is truthy at filter time, survives, is then interpolated to `''`, and is passed into the shard splitting/execution loop as a blank query. To preserve the old contract the filters should run on the interpolated result (or the interpolated expr should be re-checked for emptiness).

sugestoes.texto: DB stub changed behaviour contract: RunCommands/QueryFramesInto/TablesList previously executed real in-memory DuckDB work and callers (parser.go TablesList, sql_command.go NewSQLCommand/Execute) rely on success. Now every call returns 'not implemented', so all SQL expressions unconditionally fail. Either restore real implementation or update consumers to handle disabled state.

enableSqlExpressions always returns false: both the if branch and fallthrough return false, so `!enabled` in ReadQuery is always true and QueryTypeSQL always errors even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. The second return should reflect the flag being enabled.

New pkg/expr/sql.DB stub returns 'not implemented' for TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, but sql_command.go:100 and parser.go:26 call them expecting real results. After replacing duck.NewInMemoryDB, every SQL Execute/TablesList fails — output never matches expected behavior.

Variable named enabled is assigned the negation of FlagSqlExpressions, so it is true when the feature is disabled — the name states the opposite of what it controls and inverts the gate. Remove the ! so enabled means enabled.

Name NewInMemoryDB promises the working in-memory DB callers in parser.go and sql_command.go expect from duck.NewInMemoryDB, but the new type holds no state and every method returns 'not implemented'. Rename to reflect stub status (e.g. NewStubDB/NewDisabledDB) or document that it is intentionally unimplemented so callers are not misled.

pkg/expr/sql/db.go provides QueryFramesInto that unconditionally returns not implemented, while pkg/expr/sql_command.go now calls sql.NewInMemoryDB().QueryFramesInto expecting it to populate the result frame. Every SQLCommand.Execute therefore fails. Implement the DB methods (restore duck-backed logic) instead of stubbing.

issues.descricao: The variable in TablesList is still named duckDB although it no longer holds a DuckDB instance.

comentarios.texto: After replacing `duck.NewInMemoryDB()` with local `NewInMemoryDB()` and removing the duck import, the local `duckDB` still carries the old implementation name though it is no longer a duck DB. Rename to `db`/`sqlDB` (as done in sql_command.go) so identifier matches code.

issues.descricao: enableSqlExpressions returns false on both branches, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression query as not implemented even when the sqlExpressions feature flag is enabled.
The variable `enabled` in enableSqlExpressions holds the negated flag value, so it is true when SQL expressions are disabled and the name states the opposite of its value.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Check returns deny from permDenialCache before trying cached perms or the DB requery, and the entry is never cleared when access is later granted. WHY: A deny cached at T blocks the fresh-DB fallback added in the same PR until TTL expiry, so newly granted dashboards/folders stay denied and the PR goal is defeated. HOW: Delete the denial key on allow (or only set/check it on the DB path miss) instead of short-circuiting unconditionally.

WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace/userUID/action/name/parent with '_' and omits IdentityType while TypeUser and TypeServiceAccount share the same key space. WHY: Two principals with the same UID string (user vs service-account) share denial entries causing false denies, and '_' in any field makes distinct tuples collide to the same key. HOW: Include IdentityType in the key and use an unambiguous encoding (length-prefix or unprintable separator with escaping).

WHAT: A denial entry is stored per (namespace, user, action, name, parent) where name/parent are request-controlled, in a local cache with only TTL expiry. WHY: Enumerating random resource names creates one entry per guess and grows memory/serialization load per user until expiry, turning a cheap deny into a cache-blowup vector. HOW: Omit if speculative — verifier to confirm local-cache bounds; otherwise bound cardinality (e.g. cap entries, hash, or cache negative action-level results only).

Comment claims permCache allows dash1 to prove permDenialCache short-circuits, but value is false so it does not allow; cached-allow path would fall through to DB and the test passes vacuously. Set the cached scope to true to match the comment and actually exercise denial precedence.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' fixture neutralises the thing under test: permCache is seeded deny (false) with no allowing DB entry, so assert.False passes even if the permDenialCache check is removed. Seed an allowing entry so deny can only come from the denial cache.

issues.descricao: The denial cache key joins name and parent folder with underscores, so different name/parent pairs can collide and a cached denial for one resource denies another until TTL expiry.
issues.textoGolden: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

comentarios.texto: The denial cache key does not distinguish underscores inside resource and parent UIDs from its field separators. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") generate the same key, so denying the first request makes Check return false for the second even if its permissions explicitly allow it. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON tuple or length-prefixed fields.

The denial cache key is not injective: for the same namespace, user and action, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. After the first request stores a denial, Check's new early cache return denies the second request without checking its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example a JSON tuple or length-prefixed components) and add a test verifying that these two requests do not share a denial entry.

Make the denial-cache key encode component boundaries unambiguously (for example, length-prefix or serialize the components). For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both produce the suffix `_a_b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs, so denying the first request caches a key that causes Check to immediately deny the second request without evaluating its permissions, even if that resource is allowed.

issues.descricao: The explicit denial-cache test seeds the cached permission as false instead of true, so it would pass without the denial-cache short-circuit and does not verify it.
issues.textoGolden: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

comentarios.texto: This test claims to prove the permDenialCache short-circuit (service.go:116-121) denies access, but it seeds the cached permission as map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} (a deny), contradicting its comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". Because the cached set is already a deny, checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to the DB path, and the fake store also returns no permissions, so Allowed stays false. The assertion passes even if the entire permDenialCache early-return were deleted. Seed the cached permission as true (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so that only the denial-cache entry can force Allowed=false; otherwise the test does not verify the feature.

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets the permCache entry to `false`, which is a deny. The test therefore does not show that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to `true`, or change the comment to match.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test would still pass if the permDenialCache check were removed. permCache is seeded with dash1:false, not true as the comment claims, so the normal path also denies. Seed permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and a store that grants the permission, so Allowed=false can only come from the denial entry.

issues.descricao: A cached permission set that denies a resource always triggers a full DB permission reload, so checks over many inaccessible dashboards issue one query per resource instead of being served from cache.

comentarios.texto: Every distinct resource denied by the cached permission map triggers a reload of the entire user's action permission set, because the denial cache is resource-specific and a cached false result always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. Sequential checks of N inaccessible dashboards therefore execute N full permission queries and cache rewrites even with a current action-wide cache; getUserPermissions' singleflight only merges overlapping requests. Bound refreshes per user/action with a short refresh cooldown or generation marker so different resource misses can share a recent refresh.

issues.descricao: The Service struct comment listing its caches was not updated for the new permDenialCache field.

comentarios.texto: The struct doc comment still reads "// Cache for user permissions, user team memberships and user basic roles", but this PR added the new `permDenialCache` field (line 58). The comment no longer enumerates what the struct actually holds and misleads a reader about the new denial-cache field; update it to mention the permission-denial cache so the prose matches the fields.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Added r.log.Error calls log the full ids slice (up to batch size, e.g. 32767 IDs) plus cond on every fetch/delete batch. WHY: Floods error logs on every cleanup cycle, creates false error alarms and huge log I/O/disk usage. HOW: Remove these debug statements or downgrade to Debug level logging only the count.

WHAT: Global cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. WHY: Runs all 8 cleanup jobs (snapshots, versions, images, annotations, invites, URLs, history) 10x more often, multiplying DB load combined with the new multi-round-trip annotation cleanup. HOW: Revert to 10 minutes or justify the frequency change separately.

WHAT: MaxCount cleanup fetches victim IDs with LIMIT/OFFSET then deletes them in a separate statement with no transaction. WHY: Concurrent deletion of newer rows between fetch and delete shifts the OFFSET window, so a fetched ID can slide back into the top-MaxCount set that must be kept yet still gets deleted. HOW: Re-check membership or perform the delete atomically if exact MaxCount retention is required.

Lines 534/537 call r.log.Error for normal progress when err is guaranteed nil (checked just above) and after successful delete. The Error level and 'err' key state a failure when code is on success path. Use Debug/Info and drop the nil err field to stop alarming and log spam
Lines 554/557 log normal count-cleanup progress at Error level with nil err, implying failure and dumping ids/cond on every batch. Demote to Debug and remove misleading err field
Lines 576/579 log routine orphaned-tag progress at Error level with nil err. Same name-vs-behavior mismatch as above; use Debug for routine trace

untilDoneOrCancelled stops when batchWork returns affected==0, but batchWork now returns RowsAffected from deleteByIDs after a separate fetchIDs with LIMIT. Under concurrent deletes the fetched IDs can already be gone so delete affects 0 even though unfetched matching rows remain beyond the LIMIT window, causing early exit with MaxAge/MaxCount/orphan invariant still violated. Terminate on fetched count == 0 instead of deleted count == 0.

issues.descricao: Leftover debug logs in the annotation cleanup emit Error-level entries with the full ID list on every batch, flooding error logs during normal operation.
issues.textoGolden: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls r.log.Error on every cleanup batch (also duplicated at lines 554-557 and 576-579) dumping full ids slice, cond, and nil err at Error level. WHY: Fires Error-level log per batch and serializes up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (32767 in new test), spamming error logs/monitoring on every normal cleanup run. HOW: Downgrade to Debug or remove; do not log full ids at Error.

WHAT: Leftover debug logging calls `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)` (and the identical Error-level logs for 'by count' and 'Tags to clean', lines 554/557/576/579) run on every batch in production. WHY: These log the full ID slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 elements) at Error severity on every cleanup iteration, flooding logs with false error noise and large payloads for a normal successful operation, and can trigger error-based alerting. HOW: Remove these log lines, or downgrade to Debug and drop the full `ids` slice (log only the count).

Avoid using Error-level logging on the normal cleanup path. The new r.log.Error calls emit count, ids, cond, and err at lines 534/537, 554/557, and 576/579 during non-error execution, creating log noise; consider downgrading or removing these logs on the normal path.

issues.descricao: The comment states SQLite's parameter limit is 999, which is only true for SQLite versions before 3.32.0.

comentarios.texto: The comment states that SQLite has a parameter limit of 999, but SQLite >= 3.32.0 defaults to 32766 (as the added integration test also recognizes). This branch is choosing a conservative compatibility threshold, not expressing the limit of every SQLite database. Document 999 as the older-version/compatibility threshold so maintainers do not mistake this constant for the actual limit on modern SQLite.

issues.descricao: On MySQL and Postgres, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID without limit, so a cleanup batch size above 65535 makes every DELETE fail.

comentarios.texto: The bind-parameter workaround only handles SQLite's limit; the placeholder branch is used for every other engine with len(ids) placeholders and no bound. The previous implementation had no bind parameters, so this path is new. Postgres (extended protocol) and MySQL both cap bind parameters at 65535, so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize larger than that makes this DELETE fail at Exec with a parameter-limit error instead of cleaning anything. Clamp the number of ids per DELETE (e.g. chunk into <=1000/<=65535 id sub-batches) for all dialects, not just SQLite.

On Postgres and MySQL, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID with no cap. A configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above the driver's bind-parameter limit (65535) makes every cleanup batch fail, and the cleanup job then never finishes. Split the IDs into chunks below the limit, or inline the integer IDs as the SQLite branch does.

issues.descricao: The SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation, which is quadratic in batch size.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: SQLite large-batch IN-list built with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop over ids. WHY: Quadratic string copying on large batches (e.g. 32767 IDs in added test) during cleanup, a background job path. HOW: Build with strings.Builder or strings.Join.

The SQLite literal-ID path rebuilds the entire accumulated string for every ID, making SQL construction quadratic in batch size. Large batches explicitly supported by this PR, including the 32,767 setting in the integration test, generate substantial repeated copying and allocation before each delete, consuming cleanup time and memory. Build the list with strings.Builder and append each formatted ID once.

issues.descricao: The cleanup service ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running every cleanup job ten times as often and increasing database load.
issues.textoGolden: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no justification. WHY: Runs all 8 cleanup jobs including the new multi-query (SELECT+DELETE per batch) annotation cleanup 10x more often, multiplying DB load. HOW: Revert to 10 minutes or justify the frequency change separately.

WHAT: The cleanup job ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. WHY: This runs all cleanup jobs (annotations, expired snapshots/versions/images, short URLs, query history) 10× more frequently, multiplying background DB load and lock contention — the opposite of the deadlock mitigation this PR targets — and appears to be a debug leftover unrelated to the described change. HOW: Restore the ticker to `time.Minute * 10`.

The cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job runs. This job also drives the annotation/tag cleanup path changed in this PR, which now fetches ID batches into memory and emits Error-level logs per batch, so running it every minute substantially increases DB load and log volume with no functional benefit. Unless a 1-minute cadence is explicitly intended, this should stay at 10 minutes (it reads like a leftover from testing).

issues.descricao: The 'running the max count delete again' test case no longer runs cleanup a second time after the PR's per-subtest seeding and cleanup, so it does not verify that a repeated max-count cleanup deletes nothing.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: New interface method int order() is abstract with no default, breaking all out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementations. WHY: Existing custom providers fail to compile/run with AbstractMethodError once this interface is updated, a binary/source contract break. HOW: Make it a default method (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }).

WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies len bytes for r/s without verifying signature.length == signLength, silently ignoring trailing bytes or throwing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. WHY: Attacker-controlled JWS RS (via ECDSAAlgorithm.concatenatedRSToASN1DER from ECDSASignatureVerifierContext.verify) with extra trailing bytes verifies as if truncated, and short inputs leak unchecked exceptions instead of verification failure.

WHAT: readSequence subtracts child TLV sizes from declared length but never requires exactly zero and never checks trailing bytes, and maps indefinite length (-1) to empty sequence. WHY: Malformed DER with over-read children or trailing garbage is accepted as valid, breaking DER strictness relied on by ECDSA conversions.

WHAT: Default/Elytron/FIPS providers all return order 200 so the reversed sort ties and winner depends on ServiceLoader iteration order, while former multiple-provider error became debug-only. WHY: Deployments with two crypto providers on the classpath nondeterministically pick FIPS vs non-FIPS and misconfiguration is hidden.

WHAT: AuthzClient.create calls global CryptoIntegration.init which initializes a static singleton only once with the authz classloader view. WHY: If called before server init with a classloader seeing only the order-100 Authz provider, the server is permanently pinned to the weak provider whose methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.
Test only checks self-consistency decode->encode->decode with same custom ASN1 codec; verify re-encoded DER with JCA Signature.verify or compare to original JCA bytes so broken encoder fails.

Dead computation: lines creating ASN1Encoder and writing rBigInteger/sBigInteger discard the result and the same encodings are rebuilt for the return value. Remove the unused statements so only the encoders used in writeDerSeq remain.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature via System.arraycopy using signLength without validating signature.length. A short/truncated concatenated signature (e.g. malformed JWS) throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of declared IOException, breaking verification with an unhandled exception. Validate signature != null && signature.length == signLength and throw IOException.

integerToBytes slices off high-order bytes without validating sign or size. A negative DER INTEGER (e.g. 02 01 FF -> BigInteger -1) is left-padded to a large positive value, and an oversized positive (>qLength bytes) is silently truncated to its low qLength bytes instead of rejected. Verify s.signum()>=0 and that bytes.length<=qLength+1 with leading-zero padding before slicing; throw IOException otherwise.

readSequence subtracts each TLV length from the declared SEQUENCE length but never checks for negative remainder or leftover bytes. An inner INTEGER whose TLV extends past the parent length makes length negative and the loop exits silently, and trailing garbage after a correctly-sized SEQUENCE (outer length < total input) is ignored because remaining bytes are never checked. Reject length<0 and trailing bytes so malformed DER signatures are not accepted as valid r||s.

issues.descricao: concatenatedRSToASN1DER encodes r and s into two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances before re-encoding them in the return statement.
issues.textoGolden: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

comentarios.texto: Dead computation: the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls allocate encoders and encode rBigInteger/sBigInteger, but their results are discarded — the returned DER comes entirely from the expression at lines 117-121, which re-encodes the same BigIntegers. These two statements have no effect and should be removed (they are a leftover from an earlier formulation).

Remove these two discarded encoder writes. Each allocates an encoder and encodes a BigInteger, but neither result participates in the returned signature; lines 119–120 repeat both writes on fresh encoders. This performs redundant encoding and allocations on every concatenated-signature conversion.

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` encode values and discard the results. The return expression re-encodes the same values, so these lines are dead computation left over from a copy-paste or refactor. Remove them.

issues.descricao: order() is added to CryptoProvider as an abstract method, breaking source and binary compatibility for existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations.
issues.textoGolden: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

comentarios.texto: order() was added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes order() on every ServiceLoader-discovered CryptoProvider via Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order). Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface (an external or separately built provider jar on the classpath) will throw AbstractMethodError at detection time, i.e. during AuthzClient.create()/server bootstrap, before any provider is usable. Giving order() a default implementation (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) avoids the binary-incompatibility.

issues.descricao: detectProvider no longer fails when several crypto providers are present; with Default, FIPS and Elytron all at order 200, ties are resolved by classpath order and a FIPS deployment can silently run with the non-FIPS provider.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: detectProvider sorts by order() reversed and silently picks index 0, removing the previous multiple-providers error. WHY: Default/FIPS/Elytron all return order 200, so ambiguous classpath (e.g. default+FIPS) now nondeterministically picks one by ServiceLoader order instead of failing fast, risking wrong FIPS vs non-FIPS crypto. HOW: only auto-ignore lower-order providers; throw when the top two have equal order().

Reject ambiguous highest-priority providers rather than silently taking the first. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order 200 in this PR, so when both are present the stable sort leaves the decision to ServiceLoader discovery order. A deployment expecting FIPS can therefore initialize the ordinary Bouncy Castle provider without an error; previously this mixed classpath failed closed. Preserve the error for tied highest-priority providers (or require an explicit security-mode/provider choice), while still allowing the lower-priority authz-client fallback.

detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. Use a stable tie-breaker (delegate to the provider name/type) or reject equal top orders instead of relying on ServiceLoader order.

issues.descricao: Claims a wrong-length JOSE signature causes an unchecked exception in concatenatedRSToASN1DER; verifiers catch it and report verification failure, as with the existing providers.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature without validating signature.length==signLength. WHY: short JOSE input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and long input is silently truncated to signLength, breaking the ECDSACryptoProvider contract (IOException on malformed) used by verifier contexts. HOW: check length upfront and throw IOException.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER never validates signature.length == signLength before System.arraycopy(signature,0,r,1,len) / (signature,len,s,1,len). A short JWS signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, breaking verification on attacker-controlled input. Validate length and throw IOException.

issues.descricao: The ES384 and ES512 tests sign with the same default P-256 key, so the converter is never tested with real P-384 or P-521 signatures.

comentarios.texto: Single default EC keypair reused for ES256/ES384/ES512: testES384/testES512 names claim larger curves but body signs with the same P-256 key and only pads to larger signLength, so full-width 384/521-bit handling is never exercised. Generate a per-algorithm keypair with the correct curve (e.g. secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) before signing.

Every case generates a default EC key rather than a key on the curve associated with the named algorithm. On the standard JDK this is P-256, so testES384 and testES512 just pad P-256 signature components to larger lengths. A converter that discards nonzero high bytes beyond 32 bytes would still pass all three cases. Initialize the key generator with the appropriate curve per case (P-256, P-384, and P-521) so the larger-component conversions are actually tested.

Generate a key on the curve corresponding to each tested algorithm rather than using the provider's default EC curve for all three tests. On the standard JDK this generates a P-256 key even for testES384 and testES512, so those tests merely pad P-256 integers to larger output lengths and never exercise actual P-384/P-521 signature encoding (including P-521's long-form sequence length).

issues.descricao: The test only checks a round trip between the two new converters and never verifies the re-encoded DER against the original signature or with Signature.verify, so mutually consistent bugs go undetected.

comentarios.texto: Tautological round-trip assertion: rsConcat2 is derived from rsConcat via encode+decode that are inverses if self-consistent, so assertArrayEquals(rsConcat,rsConcat2) passes even if both directions are wrong. Verify against external oracle: Signature.initVerify + verify(asn1Des) and/or compare rsConcat to expected split, not just to itself.

The test only checks self-consistency: it asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(g(asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign))) == asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign), i.e. that concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a right inverse of asn1derToConcatenatedRS. It never compares against the original DER `sign`, never verifies the ECDSA signature, and never asserts the emvider output is canonical DER. Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

The assertion only establishes agreement between the two new conversion routines, not correctness of the converted signature. For example, swapping r and s in both routines makes this entire round trip pass, although the DER result no longer verifies the signed data. Verify `asn1Des` with the public key and original data (or compare against an independently specified encoding) so mutually compensating conversion defects fail the test.

issues.descricao: getBouncyCastleProvider in AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns the JDK default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle, contrary to the CryptoProvider contract.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Global canManage() grants manage permission when caller has only VIEW scope. WHY: Allows a viewer with all-groups VIEW to pass requireManage() gates and create/manage groups (privilege escalation). HOW: Check only MANAGE scope for manage, e.g. hasPermission(null, MANAGE).

WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes authz resource UUID instead of group ID to hasPermission and granted set. WHY: Breaks view-members filtering — UsersResource GROUPS attribute gets wrong IDs so user search/count returns empty/wrong results. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() (group ID per AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup) for both check and add.

WHAT: canView(user)/canManage(user) dropped ADMIN role from hasOneAdminRole check. WHY: Admins relying on ADMIN role lose view/manage access (denial) diverging from prior contract and V1 behavior. HOW: Restore AdminRoles.ADMIN in the role checks or prove ADMIN is handled elsewhere.
The Javadoc for requireManageMembers states it throws if canManageMembership returns false, duplicating requireManageMembership doc. Name and link disagree; should reference canManageMembers.
The @return documents Stream of IDs but signature returns Set<String>. Prose describes return shape function does not produce; change to Set.
hasPermission falls back to getResourceTypeResource which can return null; dereferencing it causes NPE/unhandled 500 instead of deny. Add null guard to return false.

Resource name is the groupId (AdminPermissionsSchema creates group resources with name=group.getId()), but this loop passes groupResource.getId() (internal UUID) to hasPermission which does findByName(server, groupId) and stores getId() in the granted set. Use getName() for both lookup and result so filtering via UserModel.GROUPS receives real group IDs and per-group evaluation hits the correct resource instead of falling back to all-groups.

Global canManage() accepts VIEW or MANAGE making it identical to canView() and disagreeing with canManage(GroupModel) which requires only MANAGE. A caller with only VIEW on all-groups passes requireManage() and can create/update groups. Require only MANAGE for the global manage check.

Producer/consumer mismatch: AdminPermissionsSchema stores the Keycloak groupId in Resource.name (Resource.id is the authz UUID), and hasPermission()/downstream UserModel.GROUPS filtering expect the groupId. Using groupResource.getId() for both the permission check and the granted set means findByName misses and UsersResource gets UUIDs that match no groups. Use groupResource.getName() on both lines.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only view permission on all groups passes manage checks such as group creation.
issues.textoGolden: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

comentarios.texto: The no-arg canManage() returns true when the caller holds only an all-groups VIEW permission (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`), whereas the per-group canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) requires MANAGE. WHAT: a caller with only the view scope on all groups is treated as having manage rights. WHY: canManage()/requireManage() gate group creation and other manage operations (e.g. GroupsResource.addGroup -> auth.groups().requireManage()), so a read-only viewer of all groups can create/manage groups — privilege escalation. HOW: drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() only returns true for MANAGE, aligning it with canManage(GroupModel): `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), identical to canView() at line 52, so a caller granted only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) correctly requires only MANAGE, and AdminPermissionsSchema defines MANAGE as the manage scope for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so the two checks disagree. requireManage() therefore succeeds for read-only administrators, letting them create/update/delete groups, add subgroups and map group roles. Drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() checks MANAGE only.

WHAT: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants global manage on VIEW scope (hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)). WHY: A caller with only view-all-groups permission passes the manage check, allowing group creation/management reserved for manage. HOW: Check only MANAGE, e.g. hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

issues.descricao: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authorization resource id instead of the resource name (the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set, so per-group view-members grants are not resolved and user filtering gets wrong ids.
issues.textoGolden: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) as group IDs and looks them up via findByName. WHY: Resource names equal group IDs (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so findByName(resourceId) misses and the returned set contains unusable IDs, breaking user search/count filtering by group. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() like V1 does (resource.getName().substring prefix / name) for both the hasPermission lookup and the granted set.

findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and granted set, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup defines resource name (not UUID) as groupId and hasPermission looks up via findByName(server, groupId). Use groupResource.getName() for both check and granted set, otherwise lookups miss to all-groups fallback and callers receive authz UUIDs instead of group IDs.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() for lookup and result collection, but V2 group resources are named with the group ID (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and hasPermission does findByName. Use groupResource.getName() in both places to evaluate the correct per-group resource and to return actual group IDs.

issues.descricao: Per-group resources are created without the Groups type, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's findByType never sees specific group grants.

comentarios.texto: findByType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) does not enumerate the specific group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, because that method creates them without setting their type. Consequently, specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group IDs used for user counts and database filtering. Assign the Groups type to specific group resources and ensure the all-Groups resource is not treated as a model group.

issues.descricao: The user search filter still requires legacy 'group.resource.<id>' resources, so with V2 group permissions the members of authorized groups are excluded from user searches.

comentarios.texto: The new V2 group permission IDs are passed into a JPA filter that still requires a legacy group.resource.<groupId> authorization resource. JpaUserProvider.groupsWithPermissionsSubquery checks for that prefixed name, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema creates V2 group resources named only with the group ID, so authorized group members are excluded from user searches even with valid group IDs. Update the database filtering path to support V2 resource naming rather than requiring a legacy V1 resource.

issues.descricao: The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers points to canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers.

comentarios.texto: The javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but this method is the require-variant of canManageMembers, not canManageMembership. The text was copied from requireManageMembership above it. It should reference canManageMembers so the documented contract matches the method name and behavior.

The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different check, so the doc misdescribes the method.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers (copy-paste). Fix link to {@link #canManageMembers(GroupModel)} so the contract describes the method it guards.

issues.descricao: The Javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a Stream though the method returns a Set.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set of group IDs.
@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission runs a full permission evaluation for every group resource on each user search and count, costing O(groups) policy evaluations per request.

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission passes getResourceTypeResource's result to policyStore.findByResource without a null check, causing an NPE and 500 on group listing and user search when the Groups type resource is missing.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is renumbered from 4 to 3 while the old value 4 is reused for FEATURE_DISABLED. WHY: Existing automation keyed on exit code 4 for recreate-upgrade misclassifies results after upgrade (3 now means recreate, 4 now means feature-disabled). HOW: Keep RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE at 4 and assign FEATURE_DISABLED a fresh code (e.g. 3) to preserve the established contract.

WHAT: testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the metadata subcommand, leaving the identical gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run unasserted. WHY: The check gate can be removed or broken without failing the suite, defeating the feature-gate coverage. HOW: Add a sibling @Launch test for the check subcommand asserting the same disabled-feature error.

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error string, never the exit code. If run() printed the message but exited 0 (or the old RECREATE code 3) the test still passes, so the FEATURE_DISABLED=4 behaviour in CompatibilityResult/AbstractUpdatesCommand is unverified. Assert exit code 4 as well.

The test launches only UpdateCompatibilityMetadata, yet the PR adds the same gate to UpdateCompatibilityCheck. Reintroducing the bug in Check (deleting its isFeatureEnabled block) would not fail this test. Exercise both subcommands.

issues.descricao: testFeatureNotEnabled only covers the metadata subcommand, so the feature guard in the check subcommand is untested.

comentarios.texto: testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the `metadata` subcommand and never the `check` subcommand. Removing the feature guard from UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() would therefore not fail any test. It also doesn't assert the exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED=4). Add a case for `check` and assert the exit code on both.

WHAT: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand disabled path and never the check subcommand. WHY: the feature gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run can be removed or broken without failing any test since no assertion covers its disabled message/exit code. HOW: also launch/assert the check command without --features (e.g. parameterize over metadata and check subcommands or add a second Launch).

testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand, leaving the identical ROLLING_UPDATES gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck unverified. If the Check gate were removed, the suite still passes. Parameterize/add a second @Launch for {UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityCheck.NAME} (with required --file or not) asserting the disabled message and FEATURE_DISABLED exit code.

issues.descricao: The disabled-feature test checks only the error message, not that the command exits with FEATURE_DISABLED (4).

comentarios.texto: The new disabled-feature test only verifies the error text, not the failure exit status. If the metadata command still prints this diagnostic but exits with 0 (or another incorrect code) instead of FEATURE_DISABLED (4), this test would still pass. Assert that cliResult.exitCode() equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED so the test actually protects the new disabled-feature failure contract.

issues.descricao: testMissingOptionOnSave only asserts a message is absent, so it would still pass if --features=rolling-updates were not honoured and the command failed with the feature-disabled error.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: createRecoveryCodesCredential never removes the credential in the non-chosen store, so re-setup leaves duplicates (new federated + old local, or new local + old federated). WHY: getCredential prefers federated but isValid can still accept the stale credential in the other store, so rotated-out recovery codes remain usable.

WHAT: After switching lookup to federated-first, the allCodesUsed cleanup still calls removeStoredCredentialById with a federated credential id, which only deletes local storage. WHY: Exhausted federated recovery codes are never removed, leaving stale state and repeated CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES prompts instead of the local-path delete behavior.

WHAT: Constructor calls credentialModelOpt.get() with no presence check, throwing NoSuchElementException when no federated or local recovery-codes credential exists. WHY: Crashes recovery-code login rendering instead of failing with a handled error, newly reachable when a storage provider accepts updateCredential but exposes nothing via getCredentials.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

issues.descricao: Creating recovery codes in external storage does not remove a previously stored local recovery-codes credential, and validation falls back to local storage, so the replaced codes still authenticate.

comentarios.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

issues.descricao: Exhausted recovery codes are removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which only covers local storage, so a federated recovery-codes credential is never removed.

comentarios.texto: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

issues.descricao: Looking up recovery codes now always queries the federated provider first, which for LDAP users adds an LDAP round-trip and can throw IllegalStateException, failing recovery-code login with a 500.
An error log in the test user storage hard-codes the credential type as 'recovery-codes' instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE ('recovery-authn-codes').

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil directly on the datetime key and value_from_cursor returns raw numeric value. WHY: The sole caller uses order_by="-datetime" so getattr returns a datetime, causing TypeError on every page with results and mismatched filter type in build_queryset. HOW: Reuse DateTimePaginator conversion (strftime to ms timestamp and fromtimestamp back to datetime).

WHAT: Negative cursor.offset is passed directly to Django queryset slicing queryset[start_offset:stop]. WHY: Django rejects any negative slice bound with ValueError/AssertionError, so an attacker-supplied cursor like 0:-5:0 triggers an unhandled 500, enabling authenticated DoS contrary to the safe-handling comment.

WHAT: The is_prev branch keeps the raw negative offset and slices the queryset with it. WHY: Django raises on negative slice bounds, so a crafted prev cursor (e.g. 0:-1:1) crashes with 500 instead of a 400, and forward clamping silently rewrites invalid cursors to page one.

WHAT: Advanced/negative-offset path is gated on has_global_access which defaults True for organization members. WHY: Any standard member with org:write can activate the vulnerable optimized paginator via ?optimized_pagination=true, defeating the intended superuser/admin-only restriction.

Allowing negative start_offset in queryset[start_offset:stop] breaks execution: Django QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError for any negative slice bound, so a crafted cursor with negative offset (reachable via ?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=) throws unhandled exception and returns 500 instead of a page. Clamp to max(0, offset) or reject negative cursors with 400.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (paginator.py:838-840) does int(math.floor/ceil(value)) which requires a numeric key, but this endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" so value is a datetime object and math.floor raises TypeError; value_from_cursor also lacks DateTimePaginator's datetime parsing. Do not route datetime-ordered audit logs through the numeric optimized paginator.

Comment states negative offsets are safe because queryset handles boundaries, but code keeps negative start_offset and Django rejects negative slicing. Prose disagrees with code; correct or remove claim and clamp offsets.

Django QuerySets raise AssertionError on negative slicing, and Python list negative slices wrap from the end. Allowing start_offset < 0 to reach queryset[start:stop] either crashes or returns tail rows outside pagination bounds. Clamp to >=0 / reject negative cursors instead of passing them through.

start_offset is clamped with max(0,offset) but the is_prev trimming check at line 192 compares len(results)==offset+limit+extra using raw offset. With offset<0 the fetched window is larger than the compared value by |offset|, so the extra-row trim never triggers (or triggers wrongly for is_prev path which still passes negative offset to slice). Use start_offset consistently or reject negative offsets.

start_offset is computed from offset (clamped with max(0,offset)) and used for slicing, but the prev-page boundary check still uses the original offset. When clamping applies the length comparison is off, causing incorrect trimming/reversing and wrong pagination results. Use start_offset in the len() comparison.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets straight into Django queryset slicing, which Django does not support, so requests with a negative offset raise an error instead of returning a page.
issues.textoGolden: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

comentarios.texto: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

issues.descricao: The comment added to BasePaginator claims negative offsets are allowed and safely handled by the queryset, but the code clamps non-prev offsets to zero and leaves prev offsets as before, so the comment misdescribes the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

issues.descricao: The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring claims streamlined boundary handling, an optimized query path and backward compatibility that the implementation, a copy of BasePaginator plus a negative-offset branch, does not provide.

comentarios.texto: Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator computes cursor keys with math.floor/ceil on the raw attribute, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so building the cursor raises TypeError for any non-empty result.
issues.textoGolden: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

comentarios.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

issues.descricao: The audit log endpoint always dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, which crashes with AttributeError for authorized token requests that have no member, even on the default pagination path.
issues.textoGolden: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

comentarios.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. Authorized non-member organization-token requests therefore raise AttributeError even when optimized_pagination is absent, instead of returning audit logs through the existing paginator. Guard the optional member and evaluate eligibility only when optimized pagination is requested.

issues.descricao: The comments and enable_advanced variable describe the optimized_pagination path as a performance optimization for administrators, hiding that it enables negative-offset slicing.

comentarios.texto: The comments describe a 'performance optimization' for 'authorized administrators', and the variable is named enable_advanced. In fact it opts into negative-offset slicing, and the optimized_pagination query parameter gates it. The names and comments hide what the flag actually enables. Rename them to say what is enabled, or remove the path.

issues.descricao: A user-controlled optimized_pagination flag lets any member with global access switch to a paginator that accepts unvalidated negative cursor offsets, widening the attack surface and causing server errors.

comentarios.texto: A user-controlled `optimized_pagination` query flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that accepts attacker-supplied negative cursor offsets. This is available to any user with global access, not only to real admins. It widens the attack surface for unvalidated cursor offsets and causes server errors. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is not backed by any check in the paginator. Fix: remove the optimized path, or have the paginator validate and clamp offsets.

issues.descricao: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets only for next cursors; a prev cursor with a negative offset is passed straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with an error (500) on every paginated endpoint.
The new comment in Cursor says negative offsets are allowed to enable efficient reverse pagination, but the constructor only calls int(offset) and provides no such behaviour.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, which is then compared against the datetime column, so next/prev cursor pagination of audit logs breaks.
Comments in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result claim Django handles negative slicing and that permissions are checked at the queryset level; both are false.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True for the errors dataset while upsampled_count is only registered in DiscoverDatasetConfig. WHY: An allowlisted errors-dataset stats query is rewritten to upsampled_count() which the errors resolver cannot resolve, failing the query instead of upsampling. HOW: Remove the errors fast-path or register an equivalent upsampled_count function for the errors dataset path.

WHAT: _get_event_stats gates upsampling on the outer closure dataset instead of its scoped_dataset argument. WHY: Dashboard-split paths execute the query against a different scoped_dataset (e.g. discover for error splits while dataset is metrics), so the gate decides for the wrong dataset and upsampling is skipped or applied to the wrong query. HOW: Pass scoped_dataset to the helper, or move the check to each call site with the dataset actually queried.

WHAT: _is_error_focused_query uses substring `"event.type:error" in query`. WHY: A negated filter `!event.type:error` still contains the substring and is wrongly upsampled, while error-only split queries like `(query) AND !event.type:transaction` contain no such substring and are wrongly not upsampled, returning wrong counts. HOW: Parse the query condition properly (handle `!`/NOT) instead of substring matching.

WHAT: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites the exact string `count()` and passes everything else through. WHY: Allowlisted queries using `count() as alias`, `eps()`, `epm()` or multi-yAxis combos silently keep raw counts, mixing un-upsampled series into results the caller treats as upsampled. HOW: Match/normalize the function name plus alias handling and extend to eps/epm (or explicitly refuse to upsample unsupported aggregations).

WHAT: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling stores any truthy float(client_sample_rate) without range validation. WHY: Values like negative, >1, inf/NaN strings become top-level sample_rate and corrupt derived sample_weight expectations in tests using error_sampling contexts. HOW: Only store when 0 < rate <= 1 and finite, catching (TypeError, ValueError) explicitly.

Presence of client_sample_rate is tested with truthiness (`if client_sample_rate:`), so a legitimate value of 0 / 0.0 is treated as missing and sample_rate is never set. Use an explicit existence check instead so 0 propagates as float 0.0

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot falsify wrongful upsampling of transactions: the fixture has no sample_weight so upsampled_count() falls back to ifNull(sample_weight,1)==1, identical to regular count(). Asserting count==1 passes on both paths.

issues.descricao: The upsampling decision is evaluated against the request's dataset instead of the scoped_dataset actually queried, so in the dashboard discover-split path (metrics dataset) error queries run against discover skip upsampling even when all projects are allowlisted.
issues.textoGolden: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

comentarios.texto: The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

issues.descricao: _is_error_focused_query uses a substring match for `event.type:error` on the request query, so negated or mixed (OR transaction) discover queries are treated as error-only and get the sample_weight sum instead of count().

comentarios.texto: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

The substring check treats `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as error-only queries. For allowlisted projects this rewrites count() to an aggregation over sample_weight even when the Discover query includes transactions, violating the error-only restriction and potentially failing against a transaction-backed query. Determine the event-type restriction from the parsed query rather than the presence of a substring.

Substring matching does not establish that the Discover query selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True here, causing count() to be replaced with the sample-weight aggregation for non-error or mixed results in allowlisted projects. This contradicts the error-only guard and can produce incorrect counts. Parse the query and establish an error-only restriction (including negation and Boolean structure), or conservatively skip transformation when that restriction cannot be proven.

issues.descricao: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being applied to transaction queries, because the transaction has no sample_weight and upsampled_count() equals count() for it.

comentarios.texto: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events would still pass if upsampling were wrongly applied to transaction queries. The transaction event has no sample_weight, and upsampled_count uses ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so the result is still 1 and 0. Give the transaction a non-default sample rate or weight so an upsampled count would differ from a plain count, or assert that the transform was not applied.
